cards.title: One-pass semi-streaming depth-first search
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform randomized one-pass streaming algorithm and fixed constants \(C\ge1\), \(k\ge0\) that, for every connected simple undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\ge1\) vertices, outputs a depth-first-search spanning tree using at most
\[C n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory, with probability at least \(2/3\) for every ordering of its edge stream?

The stream lists each edge once, contains no deletions, and can only be scanned from beginning to end. The algorithm may choose the root and neighbor order of the DFS tree. The question concerns the memory and pass bounds, with no additional polynomial-time requirement.

source_formulation.text: The 2020 paper explicitly asks whether DFS-tree computation needs more than one pass with semi-streaming memory. It treats connected simple undirected graphs and distinguishes insertion-only lower bounds from stronger insertion-deletion upper bounds.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the abstract and introduction, with the source model from p.34:3; replaces the truncated extraction

cards.why: DFS is a basic graph decomposition tool whose required ancestor structure is stronger than connectivity or an arbitrary spanning tree. Resolving its one-pass feasibility would explain whether near-linear memory can retain enough information for this globally constrained traversal without revisiting edges.
cards.status_note: The exact one-pass question is explicitly open in the checked STACS 2020 source, and the 2024 engineering paper records the existing many-pass bounds rather than a general one-pass algorithm. Current status is uncertain: the introduction of Konrad–Trehan, ESA 2025 p.22:2 (also arXiv:2508.16022v1), states that subquadratic-space BFS/DFS algorithms do not exist, citing Cormode–Dark–Konrad 2019 and Assadi–Chen–Khanna 2019. On 16 September 2026 this review followed both citations; their inspected statements establish maximal-independent-set lower bounds, and text searches and relevant theorem readings did not locate a DFS lower bound or a reduction supporting the assertion. The 2025 statement is not used as a verified resolution, but the conflict prevents a confident current-open certification. Bounded additional searches located no matching theorem. This is a completed formulation and evidence review with its status limit retained.

The long-path paper contains a conflicting introductory DFS lower-bound assertion. Following its two citations located maximal-independent-set results, without identifying a theorem resolving this DFS question. This review does not certify that assertion.

cards.definitions:
The graph has labelled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), is connected and undirected, and has no self-loops or parallel edges. The algorithm is given \(n\) in advance. Its input stream is an arbitrary permutation of the edges \(\{u,v\}\in E\), represented by the two binary vertex labels, followed by an end marker. No adjacency lists, neighbor-query oracle, random access to the graph or second scan are available. The empty stream for \(n=1\) is valid. The requirement is a promise on these well-formed connected graph streams; recognition of the promise is not an additional task.

A rooted spanning tree \(T\) consists of a root \(r\in V\) and one parent in \(V\) for each other vertex, with every parent edge belonging to \(E\). Following parents must reach \(r\) and visit no cycle. A vertex \(u\) is an ancestor of \(v\) when it lies on the tree path from \(r\) to \(v\). The required DFS condition is
\[\forall\{u,v\}\in E:\quad u\text{ is an ancestor of }v\ \text{or}\ v\text{ is an ancestor of }u.\]
For undirected graphs this characterizes a spanning tree obtainable by depth-first search: start at the root, recursively finish exploring a newly discovered neighbor before exploring another, and retain the edges used for first discovery. The root and each vertex's order of neighbors may be chosen by the algorithm. No prescribed or lexicographic traversal must be reproduced, and the neighbor order need not equal edge-arrival order. An arbitrary spanning tree need not satisfy the ancestor condition.

The output is an explicit root and parent table on all \(n\) labels; for \(n=1\), the sole vertex is the root. It has \(O(n\log(n+2))\) bits. The output may be produced after the stream ends using only retained memory and fresh randomness. A write-only output tape cannot be reread as extra storage. Deferring the output to the end does not change semi-streaming feasibility: an earlier root/parent output of this size could instead be retained within the same asymptotic memory regime.

The algorithm has a single finite description, independent of \(n\) and of the graph. It processes the input in one left-to-right pass and may keep at most \(C n(\log_2(n+2))^k\) bits at any time, including retained edges, summaries, counters, random seeds, temporary computation and postprocessing. The bound is worst case over valid streams and random choices. No advice or external writable storage is allowed. Fresh fair random bits are independent of the graph and edge order; old random bits can be accessed again only if retained within the memory bound. The algorithm must finish processing and produce an output with probability one, but no numerical bound on its processing time is imposed. In particular, the question does not silently add efficient offline computation to the streaming space restriction.

For every fixed \(G\) and every fixed edge permutation chosen before the random bits, the probability that the entire root/parent table is a valid DFS tree must be at least \(2/3\). An invalid tree or failure symbol counts as failure. Deterministic algorithms are allowed as a special case. This is a guarantee on arbitrary graphs and orders, not on random graphs or random-order streams.

Semi-streaming space here means \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) bits with one fixed exponent. A word of \(O(\log n)\) bits changes only that exponent, but arbitrary-precision words do not have unit storage cost. The source studies both insertion-only and insertion-deletion streams and states its lower-bound convention for insertion-only streams. This card retains the one-pass question in that basic insertion-only setting. A result only for streams with deletions would not refute it, while an algorithm handling deletions would be a stronger positive result.

A negative answer means that no pair of constants \(C,k\) and no such randomized algorithm works on every promised stream. It need not establish a full quadratic-space lower bound: any lower bound excluding \(n(\log n)^k\) for every fixed \(k\) would suffice. Extra passes, a restriction to sparse graphs with \(O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) edges, or a prescribed traversal order change the problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its logical negation in the stated insertion-only streaming model. A positive answer must prove that one algorithm makes one pass, respects its worst-case bit-space bound including postprocessing, terminates with probability one, and outputs some valid DFS tree with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid graph and edge order. A negative answer must exclude all fixed polylogarithmic exponents and all allowed randomized algorithms, without relying on a processing-time limitation absent from the model. A lower bound only for a prescribed traversal, directed graphs, streams with deletions or deterministic algorithms does not suffice. Experiments, random-graph guarantees, and a many-pass algorithm do not settle the target. The output is exact; numerical tolerance does not apply.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary depth-first search takes linear time when the entire graph is available in memory. The challenge here is that edges needed later in the traversal may have already passed by, and the full dense graph cannot be retained.

Finding some spanning tree is possible with near-linear memory in one pass. A DFS tree has the additional global ancestor condition: every edge must connect comparable vertices in the rooted tree. On a triangle, a star rooted at its center is a spanning tree but is not a DFS tree, because the two leaves are adjacent.

The source’s Theorem 4 gives a deterministic insertion-only algorithm with \(p\) passes and \(\widetilde O(n^2/p^2)\) bits, for \(1\le p\le\sqrt n\). At \(p\) of order \(\sqrt n\), this yields semi-streaming space, while at one pass its bound is quadratic. The quoted draft missed this improvement from the very paper containing the question.

For insertion-deletion streams the same theorem gives a randomized \(\widetilde O(n^3/p^4)\)-space tradeoff. That is a different input model. Neither tradeoff establishes a one-pass semi-streaming algorithm or a matching impossibility theorem for the target here.

The 2024 engineering paper evaluates practical versions and heuristics, often observing only one or a few passes, and discusses special random-graph behavior. These observations help explain practical relevance but do not give a one-pass worst-case guarantee on arbitrary edge orders.

Current-status evidence has a specific unresolved conflict: the 2025 long-path paper’s introduction asserts a quadratic-space obstruction for BFS/DFS, while the two papers cited there establish maximal-independent-set lower bounds in the inspected statements. No DFS lower-bound theorem or reduction supporting that assertion was located in those references. The card therefore records uncertainty rather than treating that sentence as a verified resolution.

cards.title: Local certificate size versus verification radius
cards.formal: Determine the worst-case certificate-size function \[F(s,d)=\max\{c_d(P):P\text{ is a graph property and }c_1(P)\le s\},\qquad s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0},\ d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1},\] in the anonymous local-verification model defined below. Here \(c_d(P)\) is the minimum number of certificate bits per vertex permitting sound and complete verification of \(P\) at radius \(d\), uniformly over all finite graphs. This asks for the whole numerical tradeoff, with pointwise absolute accuracy \(1/100\), rather than only a yes-or-no answer to the source’s proposed inverse-radius scaling.

source_formulation.text: Is it true that if we allow the verification algorithm to look at distance d, then the optimal size is at most \(\alpha  \cdot  s/d [\ldots ]\)

cards.why: Local certificates let every vertex check a global claim using a small neighborhood. Understanding their dependence on verification radius would distinguish properties for which additional communication reliably reduces stored proof information from properties that retain an irreducible local memory cost.
cards.status_note: The inverse-radius question is explicitly open in the 2024 source. This card documents a selected anonymous branch and a stronger full-function target. Checked later radius-reduction, certification-landscape and local-advice results do not determine it; later checks through 2026-09-16 are bounded.

cards.definitions:
Graphs are finite, nonempty, simple and undirected; they may be disconnected and have arbitrary degree. A graph property \(P\) is a set of these graphs invariant under graph isomorphism. Vertices have no identifiers, port numbers, input labels, advice or knowledge of the graph order. Graph distance is the minimum number of edges in a path; vertices in different components have infinite distance.

Fix integers \(d\ge1\) and \(b\ge0\). A certificate assignment is any function \(z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\); for \(b=0\) there is one empty certificate. At a root \(v\), the radius-\(d\) view consists of the root, all vertices at distance at most \(d\), their certificates, and precisely the graph edges with at least one endpoint at distance at most \(d-1\) from \(v\). Edges between two vertices at distance exactly \(d\) are not visible. Neither edges leading beyond the view nor the degrees of its boundary vertices outside the view are additional input.

A verifier is one finite deterministic Turing-machine program accepting or rejecting a view. A view is encoded by its finite adjacency matrix, root index and certificate strings; the decision must be invariant under all renumberings of that encoding. Thus encoding indices convey no persistent identifiers. The program halts on every finite view. Its running time and memory are unrestricted, and it may depend on \(P,d,b\), but it is the same program for every graph order and every vertex. It has no oracle, random bits or additional input.

Such a verifier certifies \(P\) with \(b\) bits when, for every allowed graph \(G\),
\[
G\in P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z:V(G)\to\{0,1\}^{b}\ \ \forall v\in V(G),\
A(\operatorname{view}_d(G,z,v))=\operatorname{accept}.
\]
The existential certificate assignment is unrestricted and may depend on the entire graph. On a graph outside \(P\), every assignment must cause at least one vertex to reject. There is no error probability. The cost is the common maximum number \(b\) of certificate bits stored at a vertex, not the total number of bits in the graph or view. Using a subset of the \(2^b\) strings is allowed.

Define \(c_d(P)\) as the least such integer \(b\), with value \(+\infty\) if no such verifier exists. The domain of the maximum in \(F(s,d)\) consists only of properties with a certificate bound \(s\) independent of graph order. Different properties and different values of \(d\) may use different verifiers; no algorithm receiving a description of \(P\) is required. The set of possible values is a nonempty subset of \(\{0,\ldots,s\}\): the property containing every graph has cost zero, and a radius-\(d\) verifier can restrict its input to radius one. Hence this maximum is finite and attained as a numerical value. All graphs, graph orders, properties and degrees in its definition are quantified; neither \(s\) nor \(d\) is hidden in an unspecified constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a mathematically specified function \(g:\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that \(\lvert g(s,d)-F(s,d)\rvert\le1/100\) for every \(s\ge0,d\ge1\). The approximation need not be integer-valued. An unambiguous expression or certified rule can specify \(g\); merely repeating the defining maximum, giving sampled values, or proving only asymptotic upper or lower bounds does not determine this function to the required precision.

context_blocks.text: Open problem 2 asks whether allowing distance \(d\) reduces optimal certificate size \(s\) to at most a constant times \(s/d\), including dependence on the parameters of local properties. It does not specify all rounding and uniformity conventions for a numerical benchmark.

This card explicitly selects the source’s anonymous model and the branch of unlabeled graph properties admitting a constant certificate bound for all graph orders. It broadens the threshold question to the underlying worst-case function \(F(s,d)\), following the authorized quantity/function review. Determining this function is a stronger quantitative target, not an assertion that it is equivalent to every version of the source conjecture. Identifier-dependent models, properties with separate vertex inputs and bounds growing with graph order are outside this selected branch.

The radius view follows Definition 15, including the omission of edges between outer-boundary vertices. A finite terminating verification program fixes computational uniformity, while local running time is unrestricted.

The source proves that anonymous radius-one certification of \(k\)-colorability requires exactly \(\lceil\log_2 k\rceil\) bits. Its larger-radius lower bound and upper bounds for selected properties illustrate the tradeoff, without establishing a universal compression theorem.

The later paper on decreasing verification radius studies how certificate sizes grow when a verifier must see less. Its bounds for that direction do not determine the cost of increasing the radius in the model of this card.

The 2025 complexity-landscape paper studies possible certificate growth rates on paths, cycles and trees, with distinctions involving identifiers and knowledge of graph order. These are different from the full worst-case function for constant certificate bounds on arbitrary graphs.

cards.title: Two-dimensional sandpile prediction in NC
cards.formal: Is the language \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) defined below in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\)? An instance explicitly supplies a finite stable rectangular array of sand grains and cells \(p,q\) inside that rectangle. Extend the array by zero to all of \(\mathbb Z^2\), add one grain at \(p\), and accept exactly when \(q\) eventually topples under the simultaneous four-neighbor rule. The question concerns one uniform circuit family with polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth for all input lengths.
cards.definitions:
Let \(W,H\ge1\), let \(B=\{0,\ldots,W-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,H-1\}\), let \(c:B\to\{0,1,2,3\}\), and let \(p=(p_x,p_y),q=(q_x,q_y)\in B\). Define \(\bar c(v)=c(v)\) on \(B\) and \(\bar c(v)=0\) elsewhere in \(\mathbb Z^2\). Set \(c_0(v)=\bar c(v)+\mathbf1_{\{v=p\}}\). With
\[
E=\{(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)\},
\]
define, for every integer \(t\ge0\) and every \(v\in\mathbb Z^2\),
\[
c_{t+1}(v)=c_t(v)-4\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v)\ge4\}}+
\sum_{e\in E}\mathbf1_{\{c_t(v-e)\ge4\}}.
\]
Here \(\mathbf1_A\) is \(1\) when assertion \(A\) holds and \(0\) otherwise. Every unstable cell topples once per simultaneous round; its threshold and the number of grains sent to each neighbor are fixed. The required output is \(1\) exactly when \(\exists t\ge0:\ c_t(q)\ge4\). All cells outside the supplied rectangle participate in the same dynamics. There is no absorbing boundary, periodic identification, missing neighbor or cell-dependent weight.

For a nonnegative integer \(z\), let \(s(z)\) be its ordinary binary expansion without leading zeros, using \(s(0)=0\), and let \(b(z)=|s(z)|\). Encode \(z\) as \(1^{b(z)}0s(z)\). A valid binary input is the concatenation of these codes for \(W,H,p_x,p_y,q_x,q_y\), followed by exactly \(2WH\) bits encoding the entries of \(c\): list rows in increasing \(y\), and within each row increasing \(x\), using \(00,01,10,11\) for \(0,1,2,3\). Dimensions must be positive and the encoded coordinates must belong to \(B\). Strings not meeting these conditions are rejected. Let \(N\) be the complete binary string length, including all array entries. Extra zero rows or columns are permitted, but their entries still count; this is not a sparse or succinct configuration encoding.

Membership in logspace-uniform \(\mathrm{NC}\) means that there exist fixed integers \(a,k\ge1\), a fixed real \(K\ge1\), and a deterministic finite Turing-machine program generating a Boolean circuit \(C_N\) from the unary input \(1^N\), for every \(N\ge0\). It must halt, use at most \(K\log_2(N+2)\) work-tape cells, and write an explicit gate-and-wire description to a write-only output tape. Its input tape is read-only. The circuit has \(N\) input bits and one output, uses AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates of fan-in one and constants \(0,1\), has at most \(K(N+2)^a\) gates and depth at most \(K(\log_2(N+2))^k\), and decides \(\mathrm{SP}_2\) exactly on all length-\(N\) strings. cards.title: Characterizing separable distances approximable in small streaming space
cards.formal: Characterize the functions \(\phi:\mathbb N_0^2\to\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\) in the domain below for which the separable dissimilarities \[d_\phi(f,g)=\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(f_i,g_i)\] admit arbitrarily accurate relative approximation by one-pass algorithms using space polynomial in \(\log(n+M+2)\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), under deletions that preserve nonnegative frequencies. cards.definitions: The domain consists of all fixed total functions \(\phi\) with \(\phi(t,t)=0\) for every \(t\geq0\), whose rational value on binary integers \(a,b\) can be computed in time polynomial in \(\log(a+b+2)\). Numerators and positive denominators are output in binary; the polynomial may depend on \(\phi\). Symmetry, the triangle inequality, homogeneity and dependence only on \(a-b\) are not assumed. A stream starts with \(f=g=0\) in \(\mathbb N_0^n\). Each item selects one vector, a coordinate \(i\in[n]\), and a change \(+1\) or \(-1\); no intermediate coordinate may become negative. The total number of updates is at most a given bound \(M\geq1\), so all coordinates are at most \(M\). Inputs \(n,M\) and a rational accuracy \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) are known in advance. The algorithm reads each update once, in an arbitrary order independent of its coins, and at the end outputs a nonnegative rational \(D\). For every valid stream it must satisfy \((1-\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\leq D\leq(1+\varepsilon)d_\phi(f,g)\) with probability at least \(2/3\); zero dissimilarity must therefore produce zero on a successful execution. The algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine that may depend on the fixed function \(\phi\). It may read fresh independent random bits, but remembered randomness, counters, work tapes and evaluation of \(\phi\) all count toward its working space. The read-once input and final write-only output are separate tapes and cannot serve as auxiliary storage. No running-time bound is required beyond termination on every run. Define \(\chi(\phi)=1\) if there are such an algorithm and constants \(B,a,b\), depending only on \(\phi\), using at most \(B\varepsilon^{-b}\log^a(n+M+2)\) working bits on every input and every coin outcome; otherwise define \(\chi(\phi)=0\). This definition ranges over all \(n,M,\varepsilon\). It does not require that a single decision program classify arbitrary descriptions of \(\phi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a noncircular necessary-and-sufficient condition on the numerical function \(\phi\), expressed without quantifying over streaming algorithms or communication protocols, and prove the classification completely in Lean. The positive direction must establish the specified approximation scheme; the negative direction must rule out every space bound of the stated form. As a function-valued benchmark answer, a supplied real-valued classification \(h\) must satisfy \(|h(\phi)-\chi(\phi)|\leq1/100\) throughout the domain. An exact zero-one characterization satisfies this tolerance. Repeating the definition of \(\chi\), covering only a proper subclass, or giving an uncertified list of examples is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The source asks broadly which distances and dissimilarities can be compressed, especially when updates can delete items. Editorial specialization: this card fixes the separable, effectively evaluable rational-valued family, one-pass nonnegative-frequency deletion model and polylogarithmic-space approximation regime. The classification function makes the domain and acceptance precision explicit without requiring an algorithm to decide the classification from source code.

The source gives a linear-space obstruction when the cost of the same coordinate difference varies too much with its offset. This explains why dependence on the vector difference is a natural candidate property, but a necessary obstruction alone does not classify all admissible functions or provide matching algorithms.

The admissible family includes \(\phi(a,b)=|a-b|\), \(\phi(a,b)=(a-b)^2\), and coordinate disagreement \(\phi(a,b)=1\) when \(a\ne b\), zero otherwise. The last is not homogeneous. Thus “must be a norm” cannot be used literally as the characterization of every dissimilarity covered by the question.

Braverman, Chestnut, Woodruff and Yang characterize a large class of sums \(\sum_i h(|f_i-g_i|)\), including nonmonotone functions, with a specific exceptional class. Their work explicitly describes this as a partial answer to the Guha–Indyk question. It does not cover arbitrary two-argument \(\phi\).

The source’s norm-sketching update concerns a geometric characterization for normed spaces and a different constant-size communication formulation. Khot and Naor subsequently show that the corresponding norm characterization fails for general metric spaces. Neither statement is a characterization of the whole streaming class defined here.

An additive error proportional to the total frequency would be much weaker when two large vectors are very close. Relative error and exact treatment of zero are therefore central to the lower bounds and must be retained. Insertion-only algorithms or summaries of normalized probability distributions have different guarantees and input models.

cards.title: Linear-round weighted APSP in CONGEST
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(b\ge1\), does there exist a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm and a constant \(C_b\) that, on every connected simple undirected \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \(\{0,\ldots,n^b\}\), outputs all exact weighted distances at their respective vertices within \(C_b n\) communication rounds, with probability at least \(2/3\) that all outputs are correct simultaneously?

The bound must hold on every execution, for all \(n\ge2\). “Linear” means \(O(n)\) with no factor growing with \(n\); a bound \(\widetilde O(n)=O(n\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) does not meet the target.

cards.definitions:
The communication network is the input graph \(G=(V,E,w)\). It has \(n\ge2\) vertices, no loops or parallel edges, is connected, and has nonnegative integer edge weights. For a fixed \(b\), each weight lies between 0 and \(n^b\) inclusive and is represented in binary. A vertex is a processor with a unique identifier in \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). It initially knows \(n\), \(b\), its own identifier, the identifiers of its neighbors and the weights of its incident edges, but no other part of the topology or other edge weights. The requirement holds for all labelled graphs and therefore all assignments of these identifiers. The usual polynomial-size identifier range is equivalent for this target because identifiers can be renamed in \(O(n)\) rounds.

Computation is synchronous. In each round each endpoint of each edge can send the other endpoint a message of at most \(B_b\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits, for a fixed constant \(B_b\). Both directions operate independently and different neighbors may receive different messages. All messages sent in a round arrive before the next round. Communication is allowed only along edges of \(G\); there are no additional links between non-neighbors. Edge weights affect shortest-path lengths, not message latency or bandwidth. Local storage and finite local computation are unrestricted and uncharged; only the number of communication rounds is counted. The local rules form one finite, computable program, fixed for all \(n\) and inputs, with no topology-dependent advice or preprocessing.

Randomized processors use independent private fair random bits. For every fixed graph, weights and identifier assignment, probability is over these bits. By the prescribed worst-case round deadline every processor must halt and produce its output; an invalid or incomplete output counts as failure. The success event requires all vertices' entire distance tables to be correct in the same execution, with probability at least \(2/3\). Deterministic algorithms are included as a special case. No average over graphs or identifier assignments is used.

For vertices \(u,v\), define
\[d_G(u,v)=\min_{P:u\leadsto v}\sum_{e\in P}w(e),\qquad d_G(u,u)=0.\]
The minimum may be taken over simple paths, since weights are nonnegative. Each vertex \(v\) must output the labelled table \(\{(u,d_G(u,v)):u\in V\}\). Distances are finite integers of at most \((n-1)n^b\); zero-weight edges and equal-length alternative paths are allowed. The output is the exact distance table, without a requirement to list every path. Output and retained local tables are local memory, not extra communication channels.

The constants, bandwidth bound and program may depend on \(b\), but not on \(n\), graph density, diameter, individual weights or the random choices. At most \(C_b n\) rounds are allowed on every execution. There is no message-count bound beyond the per-edge per-round bandwidth. The source's linear-time question is retained literally. The explicit bounded-error convention uses one fixed constant global success probability; it does not impose an additional failure probability tending to zero with \(n\). The source's nonnegative polynomially bounded integer-weight setting includes the zero-weight edges used in its lower-bound example.

The proposition's negation says that for some fixed \(b\), no such uniform bounded-error algorithm has a linear worst-case round bound on all instances. It does not demand an \(\Omega(n^{1+\delta})\) lower bound for a fixed positive \(\delta\); a rigorously unavoidable unbounded logarithmic or slower factor could already refute linear time. The notation \(\widetilde O(n)\) suppresses polylogarithmic factors and therefore must not be read as \(O(n)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated linear-round existence proposition. A positive answer must give, for every fixed weight exponent \(b\), a uniform protocol with the stated bandwidth, worst-case \(C_b n\) deadline and simultaneous exact correctness probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. A negative answer must rule out every such protocol for at least one fixed \(b\), preserving the communication and randomness conventions. A near-linear bound with an unbounded factor, approximate distances, a result only for unweighted graphs, a deterministic-only lower bound, or an algorithm with communication links outside the input graph is insufficient. Neither an expected-time bound alone nor a per-vertex success probability alone supplies the stated guarantee. The target is exact asymptotic linearity; numerical error tolerance does not apply.

context_blocks.text: Every node needs an entire row of the distance matrix, yet communication occurs only through the original network. The task therefore combines many shortest-path computations that compete for the same bounded-capacity links.

The 2017 source proves an \(\Omega(n)\) lower bound even on a weighted graph with a constant hop diameter. Its example encodes many edge weights that must pass through one communication link. Thus dependence on the network diameter alone cannot describe the cost of this problem.

The same source shows that its standard two-party reduction with a fixed partition of the vertices cannot yield a superlinear weighted-APSP lower bound. This is a theorem about the scope of that reduction framework, not an \(O(n)\) algorithm or a general impossibility of stronger lower bounds.

Bernstein and Nanongkai subsequently obtain a randomized Las Vegas \(\widetilde O(n)\)-round algorithm for exact weighted APSP, with additional generality including directed inputs. Their analysis retains polylogarithmic overhead, so it resolves the near-linear question without establishing the literal linear bound of this card.

The 2025 message-complexity paper still cites that \(\widetilde O(n)\) randomized round bound. Its own weighted-APSP result uses \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) messages and \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) rounds. Minimizing total messages and eliminating the logarithmic overhead in rounds are different objectives.

A resolution would determine whether the information-transfer lower bound fully captures exact weighted distance computation, or whether coordinating distance information imposes an additional asymptotic cost. The remaining gap concerns factors suppressed by near-linear notation, rather than the large polynomial gap present in 2017.

The same source shows that its standard two-party reduction with a fixed partition of the vertices cannot yield a superlinear weighted-APSP lower bound. This is a theorem about the scope of that reduction framework, not an \(O(n)\) algorithm or a general impossibility of stronger lower bounds.

Bernstein and Nanongkai subsequently obtain a randomized Las Vegas \(\widetilde O(n)\)-round algorithm for exact weighted APSP, with additional generality including directed inputs. Their analysis retains polylogarithmic overhead, so it resolves the near-linear question without establishing the literal linear bound of this card.

The 2025 message-complexity paper still cites that \(\widetilde O(n)\) randomized round bound. Its own weighted-APSP result uses \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) messages and \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) rounds. Minimizing total messages and eliminating the logarithmic overhead in rounds are different objectives.

A resolution would determine whether the information-transfer lower bound fully captures exact weighted distance computation, or whether coordinating distance information imposes an additional asymptotic cost. The remaining gap concerns factors suppressed by near-linear notation, rather than the large polynomial gap present in 2017.

cards.title: Maximum independent set in the congested clique
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the minimum worst-case round complexity \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)\) for computing an exact maximum independent set of an arbitrary simple undirected graph on \(n\) labelled vertices in the deterministic unicast congested clique defined below. The output is distributed: each processor outputs the membership bit of its own vertex in one common maximum independent set. Local computation and storage have no resource bound, but each local computation must terminate. Only synchronous communication rounds are charged.
cards.definitions: For every integer \(n\ge2\), the vertices and processors have identifiers \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). An input is a simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E)\), represented at processor \(v\) by its \(n\)-bit incident-edge row. Initially each processor knows only this row, its own identifier, \(n\), all identifiers and the common protocol; it has no information about edges not incident to it. The communication network is complete, independently of \(E\). Let \(b(n)=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). In each round and for each ordered pair of distinct processors, the sender supplies one \(b(n)\)-bit string; shorter payloads must use a fixed padded encoding within that string. Different recipients may receive different strings. All messages for a round depend only on the initial state and messages from earlier rounds, and arrive simultaneously at its end. Local computations are deterministic, with finite descriptions and arbitrary finite local memory; no random coins, advice depending on the input graph, or additional communication channel are available. For fixed \(n\), a protocol may depend on \(n\), but it must work for every labelled graph of that size. All processors must produce their final bits after at most its round bound; their set \(S\) must satisfy both independence, \(\{u,v\}\notin E\) for all distinct \(u,v\in S\), and optimality, \(|S|\ge |I|\) for every independent \(I\subseteq[n]\). Ties between maximum sets are unrestricted, provided the output bits describe one such set. Define \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)\) as the least integer round bound of any such protocol, taking the worst case over all input graphs. There is no promise on density or graph structure. This retains the earlier card’s deterministic, logarithmic-bandwidth specialization of the source’s broader question with bandwidth \(b\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous nonnegative asymptotic function \(f(n)\), a computably specified family of correct deterministic protocols, and a complete Lean-checked proof of constants \(c,C>0\) and \(n_0\ge2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\), the supplied protocol uses at most \(Cf(n)\) rounds on every input graph, while every correct protocol for that size needs at least \(cf(n)\) rounds on some graph. Thus \(T_{\mathrm{MaxIS}}(n)=\Theta(f(n))\) in precisely the stated model. The upper-bound family must be described by one finite procedure taking \(n\), whose local computation is uncharged. Logarithmically separated bounds, a conditional lower bound alone, approximate solutions, or maximal rather than maximum independent sets are insufficient. This is an asymptotic communication-complexity target; the numerical absolute-error convention does not apply to its big-Theta bounds.
cards.why: Exact independent set separates the cost of learning a global optimum from the cost of computing it once the input is known. The complete communication network removes distances and narrow cuts, yet each link still carries only logarithmically many bits. A tight characterization would identify whether this canonical optimization problem intrinsically requires substantially more information exchange than easier graph tasks in the same network. The circuit connections also make it a meaningful test of the limits of current distributed lower-bound methods.

cards.title: Bipartite maximal matching with polynomial-in-degree volume
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\), \(k\in\mathbb N\) and one uniform deterministic local-query algorithm which, on every finite simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), answers each vertex query after visiting at most \(C(\Delta+1)^k\) distinct vertices, such that all answers together specify one maximal matching? A proper two-coloring of the input graph is supplied. The bound has no dependence on the number \(n\) of graph vertices.
cards.definitions: The input is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\ge1\), an integer bound \(\Delta\ge1\) with \(\deg(v)\le\Delta\) for all vertices, an injective identifier map \(V\to[n^2]\), and a proper coloring \(\chi:V\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(\chi(u)\ne\chi(v)\) on every edge. At each vertex \(v\), the incident edges have an arbitrary fixed bijective port numbering by \(\{1,\ldots,\deg(v)\}\); the two endpoints’ port numbers need not agree. A query rooted at \(v\) initially knows only \(n,\Delta\), the identifier, degree and color of \(v\), and its port index set. Its visited set starts as \(\{v\}\). It can adaptively probe port \(j\) of any visited vertex \(w\), thereby learning the corresponding neighbor \(u\), its identifier, degree, color and the reciprocal port of that edge at \(u\). This adds \(u\) to the visited set. Revisited vertices are recognized by their identifiers and counted only once. A probe does not reveal unvisited vertices behind other ports. The explored vertices form a connected set; direct probes of arbitrary identifiers are forbidden. The volume is the number of distinct visited vertices, including the root, at termination. Temporary memory and local computation are unrestricted but finite. Each rooted query starts afresh, with no preprocessing, shared mutable state or information retained from earlier queries. One finite deterministic program must work for all sizes, degree bounds, graphs, identifier assignments, port orders and supplied proper colorings. It receives no advice or randomness. It outputs either an unmatched symbol \(\bot\) or one local port at its root. For the outputs to describe a matching, whenever \(v\) selects its port leading to \(u\), the separate query at \(u\) must select the reciprocal port leading to \(v\). Let \(M\) be the selected undirected edges. Maximality requires that every edge in \(E\) has an endpoint incident to an edge of \(M\). Equivalently, no further edge can be added to \(M\) while keeping all selected edges vertex-disjoint. Maximum cardinality is not required. The same matching must result for every order of queries, and repeating a query must give the same answer. The constants \(C,k\) are independent of all input parameters, including \(\Delta\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction and correctness/volume proof for the quantified algorithm, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A negative result must rule out every universal polynomial degree bound for every correct uniform deterministic algorithm in this connected, stateless model. An algorithm with a factor depending on \(n\), randomized or expected volume guarantees, an oracle allowing arbitrary jumps, a method requiring preprocessing, or an approximation to maximum matching that need not be maximal does not establish the positive statement. A linear-in-degree lower bound alone does not establish the negative statement.
cards.why: This asks how much graph information is needed to answer a single matching query while remaining consistent with all other answers. A polynomial degree bound would give a deterministic local oracle for a basic graph primitive with cost independent of graph size. A superpolynomial lower bound would separate this information requirement from the known linear dependence on degree in communication rounds.

importance.reason: A fundamental maximal-matching oracle question that isolates degree dependence and the difference between distance and volume. It asks for a qualitative polynomial-versus-superpolynomial classification with no network-size term.

cards.definitions: An LCL specification consists of an integer \(\Delta\ge1\), a radius \(r\ge1\), finite nonempty input and output alphabets \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{in}},\Sigma_{\mathrm{out}}\), and a finite list \(\mathcal C\) of permitted rooted radius-\(r\) neighborhoods with both input and output labels on every incidence \((v,e)\) where vertex \(v\) is an endpoint of edge \(e\). A radius-\(r\) neighborhood is the subgraph induced by vertices at graph distance at most \(r\) from its root; labels on incidences of its included edges are retained. An output is legal if every such rooted neighborhood is isomorphic to one in \(\mathcal C\), preserving roots and input/output labels. Identifiers, the parameter \(N\), and communication-port numbers are not part of this legality test. The problem must have a legal output for every connected simple graph of degree at most \(\Delta\) with every assignment of input incidence labels. All parts of the specification are fixed independently of the input size. Each vertex is a processor; each incident edge has a distinct local port number in \(\{1,\ldots,\deg(v)\}\), chosen arbitrarily. Initially a vertex knows only \(N\), its degree, its ports and its own incidence input labels, together with its identifier in the deterministic model. Communication uses only graph edges. In one synchronous round each vertex sends a separate message to each neighbor using only its state before the round; messages arrive at its end. LOCAL permits any finite message length. A CONGEST algorithm has a fixed integer bandwidth constant \(\beta\ge1\) and sends one padded string of at most \(\lceil\beta\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) bits per directed edge per round; the bound includes all protocol data. Local computation and memory are uncharged but finite and terminating, and each algorithm has one finite program independent of \(N\). The deterministic LOCAL algorithm must work for every injective assignment of identifiers from \(\{1,\ldots,N^3\}\). The randomized CONGEST algorithm receives no identifiers and uses mutually independent fair private random bits at the vertices, with some finite computable bound \(h_B(N)\) on the number used per vertex. It must finish within a deterministic round bound on every coin sequence, and for each graph, port assignment and input labeling, the probability that all output neighborhoods are legal is at least \(1-1/N\). Outputs are labels on the processor’s own incidences. Let \(t_B(N)\) be the maximum rounds until all vertices output, over all such inputs of size at most \(N\) and all coins. The claimed separation means there is one LOCAL algorithm and constant \(C\) with round bound \(C\log_2(N+2)\) for every \(N\), and, for every correct randomized CONGEST algorithm \(B\) with any fixed \(\beta\), there exist \(c_B>0,N_B\) such that \(t_B(N)\ge c_BN\) for all integers \(N\ge N_B\). The constants in the lower bound may depend on \(B\) and its bandwidth, but \(\Pi,\Delta,r\) and the alphabets are fixed first.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean either establishing this existence statement or proving its negation. An affirmative answer must provide the complete finite LCL specification, prove total solvability, give the deterministic logarithmic-round LOCAL algorithm, and prove the linear worst-case CONGEST lower bound against every randomized algorithm in the stated error and bandwidth model. A lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, a lower bound on a promised subfamily without a total LCL on all bounded-degree inputs, or an \(\Omega(N/\log N)\) bound does not meet the target. A negative answer must exclude every qualifying LCL, not merely the existing construction. No numerical tolerance replaces the required asymptotic bounds.

context_blocks.text: The 2021 paper establishes equality between LOCAL and CONGEST complexities for LCLs on trees, and a separation on general bounded-degree graphs. Its explicit open question asks whether the gap can extend from logarithmic LOCAL time to linear CONGEST time. The authors’ known example has an \(O(\log N)\) deterministic LOCAL algorithm and an \(\Omega(\sqrt N/\log^2 N)\) randomized CONGEST lower bound. It establishes a genuine bandwidth effect but falls short of the linear lower bound requested here.

Arbitrary input labels and every connected graph up to the degree bound are part of the problem domain. Restricting the network to a specially chosen family would remove a central part of the LCL requirement. The graph size, identifiers and random bits also cannot be encoded into a growing output alphabet, since the specification must be finite and fixed.

The source defines randomized algorithms without identifiers and deterministic algorithms with polynomially bounded identifiers. It also requires a deterministic round bound and high global success probability. The card fixes those conventions explicitly; the paper’s discussion explains that randomized identifier generation can bridge the common identifier conventions, with a change in failure probability.

Cruciani, Das, Raevskaya and Suomela’s 2026 work studies robustness of LCL definitions under local reductions. Its stated translation results concern formalism and local simulation overhead, rather than a logarithmic-versus-linear LOCAL–CONGEST theorem. They do not resolve this target.

cards.context:
The 2021 paper establishes equality between LOCAL and CONGEST complexities for LCLs on trees, and a separation on general bounded-degree graphs. Its explicit open question asks whether the gap can extend from logarithmic LOCAL time to linear CONGEST time. The statement here retains that stronger endpoint rather than counting any superpolylogarithmic gap as success.

The authors’ known example has an \(O(\log N)\) deterministic LOCAL algorithm and an \(\Omega(\sqrt N/\log^2 N)\) randomized CONGEST lower bound. It establishes a genuine bandwidth effect but falls short of the linear lower bound requested here.

Arbitrary input labels and every connected graph up to the degree bound are part of the problem domain. Restricting the network to a specially chosen family would remove a central part of the LCL requirement. The graph size, identifiers and random bits also cannot be encoded into a growing output alphabet, since the specification must be finite and fixed.

The source defines randomized algorithms without identifiers and deterministic algorithms with polynomially bounded identifiers. It also requires a deterministic round bound and high global success probability. The card fixes those conventions explicitly; the paper’s discussion explains that randomized identifier generation can bridge the common identifier conventions, with a change in failure probability.

Cruciani, Das, Raevskaya and Suomela’s 2026 work studies robustness of LCL definitions under local reductions. Its stated translation results concern formalism and local simulation overhead, rather than a logarithmic-versus-linear LOCAL–CONGEST theorem. They do not resolve this target.

cards.title: Lifting CSP sketching resistance to sublinear streaming resistance
cards.formal: For every finite family \(\Pi\) of Boolean predicates of a fixed arity, does the following implication hold? If no \(o(\sqrt n)\)-bit sketching algorithm nontrivially approximates Max-CSP(\(\Pi\)), then no \(o(n)\)-bit single-pass streaming algorithm nontrivially approximates it. Nontrivial approximation, sketching and the polynomial stream-length convention are defined below.
cards.why: A universal implication would upgrade a broad sketching classification to a fundamental limitation on all small-memory streaming algorithms. A counterexample would show that some CSPs admit an informative sequential summary even though every substantially smaller mergeable summary is approximation resistant.
cards.status_note: The 2025 source states this as a conjecture. A substantial April 2026 theorem now gives LP-gap-based linear-space lower bounds, but the checked text does not explicitly establish or refute Conjecture 8 for every sketching-resistant family. Status remains uncertain rather than certifying that the 2025 question survives that theorem. The card’s mathematical statement is complete, and its polynomial-length convention is identified explicitly.

cards.definitions: Fix an integer \(k\geq1\) and a nonempty finite family \(\Pi\subseteq\{\pi:\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}\}\). A constraint on \(n\geq k\) variables consists of a predicate \(\pi\in\Pi\) and an ordered tuple of \(k\) distinct indices in \([n]\). An instance \(\Phi\) is a nonempty list of such constraints; repetitions are allowed and every occurrence has unit weight. For an assignment \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), its value is the fraction of constraint occurrences it satisfies, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) is the maximum over assignments. Let \(\rho(\Pi)=\inf_{n\geq k,\Phi}\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\). Padding with unused variables makes this the limiting trivial approximation threshold. A nontrivial approximation has a fixed \(\delta>0\), with \(\rho(\Pi)+\delta\leq1\), and outputs a value \(v\) satisfying \((\rho(\Pi)+\delta)\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\leq v\leq\operatorname{OPT}(\Phi)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every instance and order. The algorithm need not output an assignment. A deterministic streaming algorithm has a finite state represented by \(s\) bits, a fixed initial state, an update map taking the current state and next constraint, and a final output map. It reads the constraint list once in an adversarial order. A randomized algorithm is a distribution over deterministic algorithms, chosen independently of the list. Local computation and the choice of this distribution are unrestricted; this is the nonuniform randomness model used for the source’s lower bounds. A sketching algorithm additionally has a state map \(K\) on lists and a binary combination map \(H\), with \(K(\sigma\tau)=H(K(\sigma),K(\tau))\) for every pair of lists whose concatenation is allowed; its updates append a singleton through this map, and its output depends only on the sketch. Randomized sketches are distributions over such deterministic schemes. Commutativity and linearity of the sketches are not separately required. Editorial length convention: an algorithmic space regime must handle every fixed polynomial length bound. Precisely, to admit nontrivial approximation in \(o(b(n))\) space means that there is one fixed \(\delta>0\) such that, for every fixed integer \(d\geq2\), there is an algorithm family for all lists of length at most \(n^d\), with worst-case state size \(s_d(n)\) satisfying \(s_d(n)/b(n)\to0\). The algorithm may depend on \(\Pi,d,\delta,n\), but not on the input list; the ratio improvement \(\delta\) does not depend on \(n\) or \(d\). The two occurrences of “no” in the conjecture negate this full definition.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every predicate family in the stated model, or give a fixed family that is resistant to nontrivial o(√n)-space sketching and a nontrivial o(n)-space streaming approximation for that family. Both parts of a counterexample need proofs. A faster approximation for a family already admitting nontrivial small sketches, or a lower bound under an additional condition not proved for all families in the premise, is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: This is Conjecture 8 of Singer’s column. It simultaneously enlarges the algorithm class and the permitted memory, while asking only whether any fixed improvement over the trivial ratio is possible. It does not claim that every approximation threshold of every CSP stays unchanged as space increases.

The sketching dichotomy gives polylogarithmic-space algorithms or square-root-space lower bounds, with a small slack in the approximation thresholds. Its definition of a sketch permits general mergeable summaries; restricting the premise to linear sketches would be a different statement.

Max-DiCut illustrates why the premise matters. Its trivial ratio is one quarter, while small sketches already give a ratio approaching four ninths. Better streaming approximations using more memory therefore do not by themselves refute the resistance implication in this card.

Singer, Tulsiani and Velusamy’s April 2026 manuscript proves linear-space lower bounds from integrality gaps of the basic linear programming relaxation. That relaxation assigns a distribution of local assignments to each constraint and requires consistent one-variable marginals on shared variables. Its ratio is not defined by the sketching premise in this card.

The same manuscript gives a tight classification for bounded-degree instances and explicitly continues to distinguish general sketching lower bounds from streaming lower bounds. Applying its theorem to Conjecture 8 requires a theorem connecting every resistant predicate family to the needed LP gap. This review does not claim that such a connection has been proved or disproved.

cards.title: Register space of obstruction-free set agreement
cards.formal: For every integer pair \(n>k\ge1\), determine \(R(n,k)\), the minimum number of shared atomic read/write registers sufficient for deterministic obstruction-free one-shot \(k\)-set agreement among \(n\) named processes with input domain \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), in the model below. Supply a real-valued function approximating \(R\) with pointwise absolute error at most \(1/100\) registers throughout this domain.
cards.definitions:
Fix \(n>k\ge1\). There are \(n\) processes with distinct known identifiers \(1,\ldots,n\); each knows \(n,k\) and initially knows only its own input in \([n]\), not other processes' inputs. A protocol may depend on \(n,k\), and is given by finite deterministic programs with unbounded private storage and no bound on finite local computation. No uniform procedure generating protocols for different \(n,k\) is required. A process may invoke the task at most once; it participates when it invokes, and may decide at most once, after which it stops. Any subset may participate.

The only communication is through a fixed array of \(r\ge0\) shared multiwriter/multireader registers with common names \(1,\ldots,r\). Every process can read and write every register. A register stores a finite binary string of unrestricted length; one atomic read returns its entire current string, and one atomic write replaces that string. Initial shared contents may depend on \(n,k\) and the protocol but are fixed independently of the input assignment and participation. All shared storage is in these counted registers. A scheduled process takes a local computation step, including invocation or decision, or performs one atomic read or write with a finite local update; no stronger shared primitive, random choice, clock, or failure detector is supplied.

An execution is any finite or infinite interleaving of such steps; a process may stop forever at any point, representing a crash, with no fairness or timing assumption. In every finite execution prefix, each decided value must be the input proposed by a process that has already invoked, and at most \(k\) distinct values may have been decided.

Obstruction-freedom requires that, from every reachable configuration, every participating undecided process \(p\) decides after finitely many further own steps if only \(p\) is scheduled thereafter. Other processes may subsequently resume, so safety must also hold under every extension. Register widths, private storage and running time are uncharged.

Define \(R(n,k)\) as the least integer \(r\) for which a protocol satisfies these requirements for every assignment of inputs and every schedule. A finite sufficient \(r\) is known, so this minimum exists.
cards.why: This measures how much shared memory is intrinsically needed for synchronization when processes may disagree on a bounded number of proposed values. Resolving the gap would connect the solvability of agreement tasks to their exact memory requirements, even under the weak guarantee of eventual progress in isolation.

context_blocks.text: The known bounds are \(\lceil n/k\rceil\le R(n,k)\le n-k+1\). The lower bound applies to named processes; the upper bound is achieved even by anonymous processes, so it also applies here. Both ends of the parameter range are determined: \(R(n,1)=n\) and \(R(n,n-1)=2\). In the interior, the general bounds can leave a substantial gap.

The upper-bound algorithm uses exactly \(n-k+1\) physical read/write registers, including the implementation of the snapshots appearing in its presentation. The resource is the number of arbitrarily large registers, not their combined bit capacity. The repeated version, in which processes solve a sequence of agreement instances, already has the exact bound \(n-k+1\); this card concerns one invocation per process.

Ellen, Gelashvili and Zhu conjecture in the preprint that the exact register requirement for \(x\)-obstruction-free \(k\)-set agreement is \(n-k+x\), for \(1\le x\le k<n\). Here \(x\)-obstruction-freedom means that all sufficiently active processes finish whenever at most \(x\) processes continue taking steps. The present question fixes \(x=1\) and asks for the full optimal function, an editorial broadening of the resulting conjecture \(R(n,k)=n-k+1\). It also accepts a determination that refutes that conjecture.

The OPODIS 2025 paper published in January 2026 still lists the same lower and upper bounds for the n-valued problem. Its results about different wait-free tasks do not close this gap. Bounds for swap or other stronger shared objects concern different computational models.

A second paper published in January 2026 continues to state the same register-space bounds while studying limitations of particular classes of impossibility proofs. It does not determine the register-space function.

The repeated version, in which processes solve a sequence of agreement instances, already has the exact bound \(n-k+1\); this card concerns one invocation per process.

Ellen, Gelashvili and Zhu conjecture in the preprint that the exact register requirement for \(x\)-obstruction-free \(k\)-set agreement is \(n-k+x\), for \(1\le x\le k<n\). Here \(x\)-obstruction-freedom means that all sufficiently active processes finish whenever at most \(x\) processes continue taking steps. The present question fixes \(x=1\) and asks for the full optimal function, an editorial broadening of the resulting conjecture \(R(n,k)=n-k+1\). It also accepts a determination that refutes that conjecture.

The OPODIS 2025 paper published in January 2026 still lists the same lower and upper bounds for the n-valued problem. Its results about different wait-free tasks do not close this gap. Bounds for swap or other stronger shared objects concern different computational models.

A second paper published in January 2026 continues to state the same register-space bounds while studying limitations of particular classes of impossibility proofs. It does not determine the register-space function.

cards.title: Triangle detection in CONGEST
cards.formal: For arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex networks, determine the optimal worst-case randomized round complexity of triangle detection in CONGEST, up to constant factors. Each vertex initially knows its distinct \(O(\log  n)\)-bit identifier and its neighbors, and may send a separate \(O(\log  n)\)-bit message in each direction of every incident edge per synchronous round. context_blocks.text: Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent. If messages had unlimited length, neighbors could exchange their complete adjacency lists in one round. The difficulty comes from fitting the relevant information through bounded-capacity edges.

For example, a vertex with many neighbors cannot simply send its entire neighborhood to every neighbor in one short message. On the other hand, most pairs of its neighbors may be irrelevant, so transmitting every adjacency list can be wasteful. An algorithm must exploit the topology to decide which information needs to move and where it can be combined.

Detection asks for one bit of global evidence, whereas listing requires the network collectively to output every triangle. A graph can contain a cubic number of triangles. Consequently, a lower bound driven by the volume of listed output does not automatically apply to detection. The near-optimal listing algorithm supplies a detection upper bound, but leaves this distinction unresolved.

The 2025 lower bound rules out every fixed number of rounds, including randomized protocols. It changes the old question of whether even two rounds are necessary into a quantitative gap. Conventional two-party communication reductions encounter barriers here, making stronger lower bounds a problem about proof techniques as well as about graph algorithms.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic-space streaming Euclidean MST estimation
cards.formal:
Does there exist a uniform randomized one-pass insertion-only streaming algorithm A and absolute constants \(C\ge1\), \(K\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), \(d\ge1\), \(\Delta\ge2\), and every stream of n distinct points in \(\{0,\ldots,\Delta\}^{d}\), A uses at most
\[K\bigl(d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\lceil\log_2(\Delta+2)\rceil\bigr)^k\]
bits of working memory and returns a rational estimate Z satisfying
\[\Pr[\operatorname{MST}(X)\le Z\le C\operatorname{MST}(X)]\ge 2/3?\]
The stream order is arbitrary and fixed independently of the algorithm’s private random bits. The output estimates total Euclidean MST cost; it need not describe a tree. For polynomially bounded integer coordinates, the required space is \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\), as in the community proposal.
cards.definitions:
The point set X consists of the n distinct inserted vectors. Coordinates are nonnegative integers given in binary, and the parameters n,d and the bound \(\Delta\) are supplied before the stream. The graph is complete on X; an edge between x and y has weight \(\|x-y\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}(x_j-y_j)^2)^{1/2}\). The quantity \(\operatorname{MST}(X)\) is the minimum sum of edge weights over all spanning trees of this graph. It is a real number even though the input coordinates are integers.

The algorithm is one fixed finite probabilistic Turing-machine program with a read-once input stream, private independent fair random bits, working tapes, and an output tape used only for the final rational estimate. An input record may be buffered, with those bits charged to memory. All retained state, counters, random seeds and postprocessing workspace count toward the space bound, on every input and every random tape. Consumed input cannot be revisited, and there are no deletions, extra passes, random-order promise, external storage, nonuniform advice or real-number registers. The machine must halt on every random tape; no separate update-time or total-time bound is imposed. The probability is over its coins for each fixed stream. The constants and exponent do not depend on n,d or the coordinate bound.

Dependence polynomial in the bit length of coordinates makes the finite-input convention explicit. In particular, for each fixed integer b and \(\Delta\le n^b\), the bound has the proposal’s \(\mathrm{poly}(d\log n)\) form. The logarithmic coordinate factor is recorded rather than silently treating arbitrary reals as constant-size words. The target allows d to grow, including \(d=\Theta(\log n)\); a bound exponential in d does not qualify. The approximation constant can be any fixed finite C. Requiring the estimate to lie above the true cost is a normalization: a two-sided constant-factor estimate can be rescaled at the cost of changing C. Neither an explicit tree nor a \(1+\varepsilon\) approximation is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm satisfying the stated memory, pass and probability bounds for some absolute finite approximation constant, or prove the negation for every such algorithm and constants. An \(n^{\varepsilon}\)-space algorithm for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\), a factor growing with n, a multiple-pass algorithm, or a lower bound excluding only constants near 1 does not settle this target.
cards.why: An MST measures the cost of connecting an entire geometric data set. A small summary that estimates this global quantity within a constant factor would clarify how much connectivity information survives a single streaming pass as dimension grows.

cards.definitions: The support of a vector is the set of its nonzero coordinates; a vector is \(k\)-sparse if its support has size at most \(k\). The norms are \(\|v\|_1=\sum_i|v_i|\) and \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\). The minimum in the statement is the sum of absolute values outside the \(k\) largest-magnitude coordinates of \(x\); ties may be broken arbitrarily. The decoder receives \(n,k\), the exact real measurement vector \(y=A_{n,k}x\), and read-only access to the fixed description of the scheme. It receives neither \(x\) nor its support, and must output all \(n\) coordinates of \(\widehat x\). The output need not itself be sparse. Measurements are linear and selected independently of the unknown signal. We use the real-arithmetic model: real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero number, square root of a nonnegative number, comparison, and access to an addressed stored entry each cost one operation; ordinary integer index operations cost one as well. The decoder is one fixed algorithm, with polynomial-size read-only advice depending only on \(n,k\), including the matrix and any preprocessing data. Reading advice is charged. Advice generation and forming the original measurement vector are outside the requested decoding bound. No polynomial-time explicit matrix construction is required. Once the scheme is fixed its decoder is deterministic and the guarantee holds for all real signals; a matrix chosen by the probabilistic method is admissible only if a single fixed choice works for all signals. For exactly \(k\)-sparse signals the right-hand side is zero, so the scheme must recover them exactly. For nonsparse signals, recovery quality depends on the entire tail and gains a factor \(1/\sqrt{k}\). Merely outputting a plausible support does not establish this robust guarantee.

The original question emphasizes achieving optimal measurement count and fast reconstruction together. Classical constructions achieve the two features separately for this error criterion, whereas some fast optimal-measurement schemes use a different norm on the reconstruction error.

The later for-all sparse-recovery work of Gilbert, Li, Porat and Strauss improves measurements and decoding for the ℓ₁/ℓ₁ formulation, and explicitly lists mixed-norm recovery as a remaining direction. Likewise, an input-dependent success probability does not imply that one random seed works simultaneously over the uncountable set of all real inputs.

Counting the output cost explains why near-linear decoding remains a meaningful target even when the number of measurements is much smaller than \(n\).

cards.title: Constant-round MIS in the congested clique
cards.formal: Does randomized maximal independent set admit a constant-round algorithm in the unicast Congested Clique? Precisely, for every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized distributed algorithm \(A_c\) and positive constants \(R_c,B_c\) such that, on every simple undirected graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), \(n\ge2\), the algorithm always terminates within \(R_c\) rounds, uses at most \(B_c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) bits per directed communication link per round, and outputs a maximal independent set with probability at least \(1-n^{-c}\)? Constants and program may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\), the graph or its maximum degree.
cards.why: The question measures how much communication exact distributed symmetry breaking needs when every processor can directly contact every other processor. A constant-round solution would establish a sharp capability of this widely studied model. A general lower bound would expose a bandwidth limitation that survives unrestricted local computation and arbitrary global coordination.
cards.definitions: There is one processor for each vertex \(v\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Initially it knows \(n\), its own identifier \(v\), the common identifier set, and exactly the identifiers of its neighbors in the input graph. The physical communication network is complete: in each synchronous round every processor may send a separate message to every other processor, even when the corresponding input edge is absent. Messages sent in a round arrive by its end. Each directed link has the stated bit limit independently; processors may send different messages to different recipients. No extra processors or initially centralized graph description are provided. All processors run the same finite program, with their identifier and local input as parameters. Local computation and local storage have no asymptotic bound, but each local computation terminates and reads only finitely many independent private fair random bits on every execution. All communication, including initialization and distribution of any shared randomness, counts toward the round bound. No graph-dependent or size-dependent advice is supplied. At termination each processor outputs one bit, defining \(S=\{v:\text{processor }v\text{ outputs }1\}\). Correctness means both \(\forall\{u,v\}\in E(G):\{u,v\}\nsubseteq S\) and \(\forall v\notin S:\exists u\in S:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\). Thus maximality means that no additional vertex can be inserted while preserving independence; maximum cardinality is not required. The probability refers to the single global event that all output bits together define a valid set. The round and message bounds hold on every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. Restricting the requested fixed failure exponent to positive integers is equivalent to allowing every fixed positive real exponent.

cards.definitions: The vertex set is \([n]\). A matching is a subset of edges with no shared endpoint, its weight is the sum of its edge weights, and \(\operatorname{OPT}\) is the largest such sum over all matchings of the graph. The input is a list of distinct edges, each represented by two binary vertex identifiers and its positive binary integer weight. The algorithm knows \(n,\varepsilon,c\). It reads the list sequentially in an arbitrary order selected independently of its random choices. A pass reads the same complete list in that same order; no deletions, changes of order, random access to earlier items, or requests for selected edges are allowed. The algorithm may stop after any number of passes up to the stated bound. At the end it must output the actual edges of a matching, not merely an estimate of its value. The empty graph has optimum zero and admits the empty output. All stored bits, including edge identifiers, weights, random seeds retained for reuse, counters and temporary working memory, count toward space. A final write-only output tape is permitted, but cannot be used as storage during the passes. The bound is worst case over inputs and random choices; success is required for each input and order. Local computation time is unrestricted, and the finite algorithm may depend on the fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Equivalently the space target is O(n) words of O(log n) bits for each fixed pair of parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) is required for the pass count or space constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of the approximation, actual matching output, pass and bit-space guarantees for every fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Alternatively prove that this family of guarantees is impossible, for some fixed parameters. A constant-pass algorithm with extra logarithmic factors in bits, an algorithm for bipartite graphs only, or a RAM approximation algorithm does not establish the displayed statement.

context_blocks.text: The 2006 page contains two questions: a constant-pass streaming approximation with O(n log n) space, and a linear-time RAM approximation scheme. This card keeps the streaming question as its single target. Editorial convention: space is measured explicitly in bits and weights have polynomially bounded integer encodings, removing an ambiguity in the historical page.

Duan and Pettie resolved the RAM direction with running time \(O(m\varepsilon^{-1}\log\varepsilon^{-1})\) for maximum-weight matching. That algorithm can access and store the graph in ways unavailable to the streaming model. The old RAM question is therefore recorded as solved context rather than repeated as an open demand.

Gamlath, Kale, Mitrović and Svensson obtained arbitrarily accurate weighted matching in a number of passes depending only on accuracy, using memory linear in n up to polylogarithmic factors. This settles the broader constant-pass semi-streaming objective, but the stated space guarantee alone does not supply the exact bit bound retained here.

Huang and Su improve the number of passes to a polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\). Their Theorem 1.2 states \(O(n\log W\,\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon))\) words, where \(W\) is the weight ratio. Under the present weight encoding this can be \(O_{\varepsilon,c}(n\log^2 n)\) bits. One must account for word size before comparing it with the target.

The 2025 overview distinguishes general weighted graphs from bipartite and unweighted cases and tabulates their different pass-space guarantees. Strong bounds for one of those restrictions cannot be silently substituted for the graph class here.

For weighted matchings, improving the objective can involve both alternating paths and alternating cycles. Retaining enough information to coordinate such improvements while storing only a linear number of words is the specific resource issue in this formulation.

cards.title: LOCAL coloring below square-root degree dependence
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that properly colors every simple n-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$ with colors in $\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}$ in $O(\Delta^{0.499}+\log^* n)$ synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct \(O(\log  n)\)-bit identifiers and know n and Delta. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The constant in the round bound must be independent of both n and Delta.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm with the specified uniform round bound, or prove that no deterministic LOCAL algorithm attains it. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent one-half does not meet the target.
cards.why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
cards.definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target.

progress.text: Maus and Tonoyan obtain $O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)$ deterministic rounds for the more general degree-plus-one list-coloring task. Ordinary coloring follows by using a common palette.
Suomela’s updated open-problem list explicitly asks whether the exponent 0.499 is attainable with Delta+1 colors and only an additive log-star n dependence.

The SODA 2026 discussion records a separate deterministic $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ upper bound for Delta+1 coloring. That bound is independent of degree but does not provide the two-parameter guarantee asked here.

context_blocks.text: A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

The target chooses a specific exponent strictly below one-half, as in Suomela’s list. The numerical improvement is small; its purpose is to cross the apparent degree barrier while keeping the optimal-size palette. Allowing more colors, randomness, or a larger n-dependent term gives separate questions.

cards.title: Randomized parity sketches versus one-way communication for XOR functions
cards.formal: Are there universal constants \(C>0\) and \(a\geq0\) such that, for every \(n\geq1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\{0,1\}\), \[R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\leq C\bigl(1+R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\bigr)\log^a(n+2),\qquad f^+(x,y)=f(x+y)?\] Here the two complexities use worst-input error and shared randomness as defined below. This fixes the polylogarithmic-loss convention in the source’s conjecture.
cards.why: A positive result would justify proving lower bounds for arbitrary one-way XOR protocols by analyzing linear summaries, a much more structured class. A separation would identify Boolean information that a short nonlinear message preserves more effectively than nonadaptive random parities.
