cards.definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_2\) has elements zero and one, with addition modulo two; vector addition is bitwise XOR. A randomized parity sketch of length \(k\) consists of a jointly sampled matrix \(A\in\mathbb F_2^{k\times n}\) and a decoder \(g\). Their joint distribution is fixed in advance, independently of the input \(z\). The sketch is the \(k\)-bit vector \(Az\); the decoder knows the sampled matrix and all shared coins, and may depend on \(f\) and \(n\). For each fixed \(z\), its probability of outputting \(f(z)\) must be at least \(2/3\). The minimum possible \(k\), including zero, is \(R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\). Each row of \(A\) specifies a subset of input coordinates whose parity is measured. Rows are chosen before seeing any measurement outcome: adaptive parity queries are not allowed. In the communication model Alice knows \(x\in\mathbb F_2^n\), Bob knows \(y\in\mathbb F_2^n\), and both know \(f,n\) and a public random string independent of their inputs. Alice sends one message; Bob must output \(f(x+y)\). For every fixed pair \((x,y)\), success probability is at least \(2/3\). The cost is the largest message length over inputs and coin outcomes; variable-length messages can be padded. Its minimum is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\). Local computation, the description of \(f\), and shared randomness are free in both models. No uniform polynomial-time construction of optimal protocols is required. Logarithms are base two. The constants in the proposed inequality are independent of the truth table of \(f\), the dimension and its communication complexity. The additive one handles zero-cost constant functions without imposing a convention for logarithms of zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed inequality with fixed universal constants, or prove its negation: for every proposed constants there is a dimension and Boolean function violating the bound. A superpolylogarithmic separation family suffices for a negative answer. Equality for deterministic protocols, average error under the uniform input distribution, or a polynomial rather than polylogarithmic loss does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: The source asks whether randomized linear sketching and randomized one-way communication of the associated XOR function agree up to polylogarithmic factors. The card spells out the usual dimension-based interpretation at error one third; it does not request exact equality of the two integer complexities.

The easy comparison is \(R^{\rightarrow}_{1/3}(f^+)\leq R^{\mathrm{lin}}_{1/3}(f)\): Alice sends \(Ax\), and Bob forms \(Ax+Ay=A(x+y)\) before using the decoder. The question is whether an arbitrary message can always be replaced, with the stated loss, by information of this linear form.

For deterministic exact computation the complexities agree. The randomized case allows a different error set for each choice of coins, so the deterministic statement does not give the desired simulation by simply fixing a seed.

Kannan, Mossel, Sanyal and Yaroslavtsev prove an analogue under uniformly distributed inputs, with an adjustment of the error constant, and analyze several function classes. Worst-input correctness is stronger: a protocol cannot ignore even a very small exceptional set of pairs.

The 2026 turnstile simulation paper concerns streams of integer-coordinate insertions and deletions. Its discussion treats modular and XOR updates as a separate line of work. A simulation for algorithms that already process long streams does not itself convert a single arbitrary Alice-to-Bob message into a parity sketch.

sentences: The output is a single estimate of the largest absolute coordinate of a streamed frequency vector.
The allowed additive error is one over k times the final L1 or L2 norm.
Insertion-only streams and signed differences of two streams are distinct modes of the same resource question.

cards.definitions: Parameters \(n,M,k\) are integers supplied in binary before the stream, together with the two flags. The frequency vector starts at \(f=0\in\mathbb Z^n\). There are at most \(M\) updates \((i,\Delta)\), where \(1\le i\le n\). In insert mode every \(\Delta=1\); in difference mode \(\Delta\in\{-1,1\}\), and update \((i,\Delta)\) replaces \(f_i\) by \(f_i+\Delta\). Negative intermediate and final frequencies are allowed in difference mode. Equivalently, positively and negatively tagged insertions describe the difference of two streams, with their combined length bounded by \(M\). Only this bound, not the actual stream length, is known in advance. Set \(\|f\|_1=\sum_i|f_i|\), \(\|f\|_2=(\sum_i f_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\|f\|_\infty=\max_i|f_i|\). The additive tolerance is scaled by the final vector, not by the total number of updates; cancellation therefore matters. At the end, output one rational number \(z\) as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. No coordinate identity or list of heavy items is requested. On \(f=0\), the success event requires exactly \(z=0\). The fixed stream is chosen independently of the algorithm’s private independent fair random bits. There is one terminal query, with success at least \(2/3\) separately on every valid stream; there is no requirement of simultaneous success at all prefixes. Use a uniform randomized multitape streaming machine with one fixed finite program for all parameters, no advice, no public random table and no oracle. The parameter header is read-only. An update is available in a read-only buffer until the machine advances to the next update, after which earlier updates cannot be revisited. Every work-tape bit, stored random bit or seed, counter, index, table and input-dependent retained state counts toward space, including all scratch space used during processing and final decoding. Input and write-only output cells do not count; copies do. Address and head-position information accessible to the algorithm that can carry input-dependent state is charged. The unreadable physical position of the one-way stream is not work memory; the number of updates already consumed is not supplied as a free clock. Random bits cannot be reread unless retained. The machine must halt on every valid finite stream and every random tape; computation time is unrestricted. Space is the maximum number of charged bits over all such streams and random tapes for the given parameters, not its expectation. Bounds may be piecewise over parameter regimes and must use ordinary asymptotic notation with all logarithmic factors exposed. The reciprocal-integer accuracy convention \(\epsilon=1/k\), finite update budget, private randomness and bit accounting make the source’s qualitative space question precise.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a tight asymptotic space characterization across the complete parameter domain and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean. It must include uniform algorithms attaining the stated upper bounds, their terminal-error and worst-case-space guarantees, and matching lower bounds for every algorithm in the same model, up to constants independent of all parameters and flags. A one-sided bound, a bound only for identifying heavy items, a word count hiding bit costs, or a result for only one norm or update mode does not determine the whole characterization. This is an asymptotic resource target: the benchmark does not apply an additive 1/100 tolerance to big-O or big-Theta bounds.

context_blocks.text: The largest absolute frequency is a scalar statistic. Identifying which item attains it can require additional information about a large item domain. The source asks whether that distinction can reduce memory when an additive error measured against the full frequency vector is allowed.

The two norms specify different accuracy requirements. For \(f=(3,-2,0)\), the target value is three, while the error scale is either \(5/k\) or \(\sqrt{13}/k\). For a difference stream, many updates can cancel, so an error proportional to the number of processed updates can be much larger than the permitted error.

This card retains both error scales and both update settings from the source as flags in one space-complexity characterization. It asks for their full dependence on the domain, stream budget and accuracy, rather than for a new yes/no claim that every historical bound remains unimproved. The exact finite-input and randomness conventions are editorial specifications.

Bhattacharyya, Dey and Woodruff explicitly report answering the insertion-only \(L_1\)-error part of the 2006 question. For maximum-frequency estimation they report \(O(\epsilon^{-1}\log\epsilon^{-1}+\log n+\log\log t)\) bits, where \(t\) is the stream length, and describe optimality in their stated regimes. Their result is recorded as existing progress, not as an unsolved insertion-only endpoint.

That result does not by itself supply the \(L_2\)-relative or signed-difference cases. In particular, insertion-only \(\|f\|_1\) equals the number of updates, whereas cancellation destroys that equality in a difference stream. A theorem’s norm, update promise, scalar versus item output, and parameter restrictions must all match before it can be counted toward the full target.

The original page explicitly distinguishes bit space from a count of machine words: random-function descriptions and counters also consume memory. The reviewed card preserves that distinction. The requested comparison is therefore about complete memory usage, not only the number of stored counters.

A full characterization would identify which memory costs arise from maintaining frequency magnitudes and which arise from recovering item names. It would clarify the value of scalar summaries for comparing streams over large domains and the cost of allowing deletions or cancellation.

cards.definitions: The communication network is a finite undirected simple graph \(G=(V,E), |V|=n\ge 2\). Every edge has a supplied direction, known to its endpoints; no acyclicity is promised. A vertex’s outdegree is its number of outgoing edges, and every vertex has outdegree at most the supplied bound \(\beta\). Its indegree and total degree may be arbitrarily large. A proper coloring assigns each vertex a label from one common palette so that endpoints of every edge have different labels, regardless of the edge direction. Vertices execute the same deterministic algorithm in synchronous rounds, have unique identifiers of \(O(\log  n)\) bits, know their incident ports and edge directions, and may know n and \(\beta\). Each round allows a separate message of unbounded size to each neighbor in either direction and unrestricted finite local computation. Cost is worst-case round count over graphs, orientations and identifiers. No precomputed coloring or graph decomposition is supplied. The function f may grow arbitrarily fast with \(\beta\), but cannot depend on n, total degree or the orientation’s path lengths. Both the exponent improvement \(\varepsilon\) and the coefficient of \(\log * n\) must be uniform over \(\beta\) and n. Here \(\log * n\) is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach a value at most one. Edgeless graphs, including the \(\beta =0\) case, can be assigned one color separately.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of the uniform deterministic algorithm with the stated palette and additive round bound, or establish that no such \(\varepsilon\), constants, computable f and algorithm exist. cards.definitions: There are n sequential processes with distinct identifiers \(1,\ldots ,n\). Each invokes a new high-level operation only after its previous one returns. The scheduler interleaves atomic shared-memory steps arbitrarily; a process may stop forever at any point. A register stores a finite value and supports atomic Read and Write. A Test&Set object is a bit initially 0 whose atomic operation returns the old bit and sets it to 1; arbitrarily many initially fresh objects and registers are available. Private computation and storage are allowed. No bound on memory growth or on the number of operations in a history is imposed, but every performed step manipulates finitely represented data. No Compare&Swap, stronger atomic multi-object operation, or queue base object is supplied. Sequential queue state is a finite sequence of values from \(\{0,1\}\)*. \(Enqueue(v)\) appends a new occurrence of v and returns an acknowledgement. Dequeue removes and returns the first occurrence if one exists; otherwise it returns a distinguished EMPTY symbol outside the value set and leaves the queue empty. Equal values may be enqueued multiple times, but each enqueue occurrence may be removed only once. Linearizability means that each finite concurrent history can be completed by responses to some pending invocations and deletion of the others, so that its completed operations have a legal sequential FIFO order preserving each process’s order and real-time order: an operation that returns before another is invoked precedes it. Wait-freedom means that any invoked operation whose process continues taking steps returns after finitely many of that process’s own steps, regardless of other processes’ speeds or failures. No promise that another process will take a step is available. The algorithm may depend on the fixed n; the question does not require one implementation for infinitely many simultaneously participating processes. Common\(_{2}\) denotes types implementable for every finite n from registers and two-process-consensus power; the cited model paper states the queue question equivalently using Test&Set. Equal consensus numbers alone do not assert mutual implementability.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct such a deterministic implementation for every finite n, or prove impossibility for some finite n in this model. Both exact linearizability and individual wait-free progress are required. A lock-free implementation that permits starvation, a restriction on the number of enqueuers or dequeuers, duplicated removal of an occurrence, weak-empty responses, bounded histories, or a stronger atomic base type does not meet the target. An impossibility result only for strong linearizability does not rule out ordinary linearizability.

references.authors: de Azevedo Piovezan, Felipe; Hadzilacos, Vassos; Toueg, Sam

cards.definitions: The system consists of asynchronous processes with distinct identities communicating through shared objects and atomic read/write registers. A process can crash by stopping permanently. Algorithms must be correct for every schedule and every pattern of such crashes. Wait freedom means each operation or task invocation of a process that continues taking steps completes after finitely many of its own steps, regardless of the speeds or failures of other processes; no fixed complexity bound is requested. Reductions are deterministic: randomization is not available. The one-shot task \(T(n,k,I)\) has at most n participating processes, each supplying an input in I and deciding once. Every decision is an input supplied by a participant, at most k distinct values are decided, and every participant that continues taking steps must decide. No sequential ordering constraint is added to these task guarantees. An \((n,k)\)-set agreement object O has ports \(1,\ldots ,n\) and an operation \(ProposeSA(v), v\in I\). Each process chooses a port for each call and waits for its response before making another call. Access is well formed if no two pending calls use the same port. Ports are not permanently assigned to process identities; arbitrarily many processes may use the object over its lifetime, but at most n calls may be pending simultaneously. Only well-formed access is required to be implemented. On every such execution, each response is the current call’s proposal or a proposal of a previously invoked call, and across the entire execution at most k distinct values are returned. This agreement bound does not reset after a round or after all processes become idle. All invocations are supported and are wait-free. A finite sequential history S is a sequence of completed triples (port,proposal,response). Determinism requires that for every allowed S, port p and proposal v there is a unique response extending S by a call at p with v; different histories or ports may give different responses. Linearizability requires every concurrent history to admit an ordering of its operations that obeys this sequential specification and preserves real-time precedence: an operation whose response precedes another’s invocation must come first. Incomplete calls may be discarded or assigned responses before ordering them. To implement an object means to produce only its allowed histories, with the required termination, for all well-formed client executions; reproducing every allowed history is unnecessary. O and T are computationally equivalent when copies of O and registers can solve T, and O can be implemented from registers and instances of any correct solver for T. A task instance has n one-shot participant roles; separate instances have independent state, and the implementation must rely only on the task guarantees, not on additional agreement power a particular solver might possess. This is the source’s equivalence to the black-box set agreement task. Any number of fresh instances and registers is allowed; a completed operation uses finitely many steps. The object’s specified initial state is fixed independently of client inputs. O already solves T by one proposal per participant on distinct ports, so the substantive issue is whether a reduction from the task to O can exist.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that no such object and reverse wait-free implementation exist for every \(n>k>2\), or refute the statement by giving a pair \(n>k>2, a\) proposal domain with at least n values, a deterministic linearizable object and a correct wait-free implementation from the set agreement task and registers. A positive proof need not exhibit a stronger set agreement task: that is an additional conjectured explanation in the source, not a required proof method. Restricting objects to port-independent behavior or proving only some parameter pairs does not establish the universal claim.

cards.definitions:
The pattern H is an undirected finite simple graph. It is 2-vertex-connected if it has at least three vertices, is connected and remains connected after deleting any single vertex and its incident edges. This excludes an isolated edge and includes triangles and longer cycles. The network G is an arbitrary finite simple undirected graph on n vertices. A copy of H is an injective map \(\varphi :V(H)\to V(G)\) such that every edge uv of H maps to an edge \(\varphi (u)\varphi (v)\) of G. Extra edges among the images are allowed: the task is not induced-subgraph detection, homomorphism, minor containment or property testing with a distance promise.

There is one processor at each vertex. Each knows n, H, its own distinct identifier and the identifiers of its neighbors; identifiers have \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits, and the guarantee must hold for every valid assignment of identifiers. Local edges have identifiable ports. In each synchronous round a node may send a different message of at most \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits to each neighbor, for a fixed constant B independent of n. Messages are received before the next round, and later messages may depend on everything received so far. No communication is allowed across nonedges. Local computation and memory are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. This is ordinary CONGEST, with distinct messages permitted on distinct edges, not broadcast CONGEST or the congested clique.

The algorithm is a uniform distributed procedure fixed with H; it may use independent private random bits at the nodes. Deterministic algorithms are included as a special case. It halts within a worst-case bound \(T_{H}(n)\) on every network, identifier assignment and random tape. The success event concerns the joint vector of all node outputs, with probability over all random bits. In an H-free network all outputs must be NO simultaneously; in a network containing H one YES anywhere suffices. There is no requirement that the detecting node belong to a copy, identify its vertices, list all copies, or notify distant nodes. Disconnected networks are permitted and the same global output convention applies.

The required bound \(n^{o(1)}\) means that one such algorithm exists with \(\log (\max \{2,T_{H}(n)\})/\log  n\to 0\) as \(n\to \infty\). Equivalently, for every fixed \(\delta >0\) its worst-case round bound is at most \(n^{\delta}\) for all sufficiently large n. Constants and the threshold length may depend on H and \(\delta\). A family of different algorithms, one for each \(\delta\), is not silently identified with that single-algorithm claim. A bound \(n^{\alpha _{H}}\) with a fixed positive \(\alpha _{H}\), even a very small one, is not subpolynomial. The size of H is a constant, not another growing complexity parameter.

The source also asks whether every 2-connected pattern instead requires a polynomial number of rounds. A theorem giving each fixed H a lower bound \(\Omega (n^{\delta _{H}})\) for some \(\delta _{H}>0\) would refute the existence question, but this stronger growth dichotomy is not assumed to be its logical negation. A negative answer here only needs to exclude the stated \(n^{o(1)}\) algorithms for every eligible H.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer provides one fixed eligible H and proves a uniform randomized CONGEST algorithm with the stated global success probability and \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case rounds. A negative answer rules out such an algorithm for every fixed eligible H. A lower bound for only one pattern, or a fast algorithm for induced copies, promised-far graphs, listing in another model or a pattern that grows with n, does not settle this existence question.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
